conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the medicine doctor taking care of you tonight. I understand you came in with left upper belly pain and nausea. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been about four days. Pain on the left upper side, and it wraps around to my left flank. I feel nauseated and full really fast when I eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Is it constant or does it come and go? And anything make it better or worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s kind of always there, but it’s better when I eat, which is weird. I’m not throwing up though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, blood in stool, or black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. No blood. No fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How about diarrhea or constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yesterday I had a normal bowel movement. Today it’s been looser, but not a ton.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any burning with urination or urinary symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the emergency department your bloodwork looked reassuring—no signs of infection, and your kidney and liver tests looked okay. Your urine test didn’t show anything concerning. We also did a chest X-ray to look for free air under the diaphragm, and it was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not like a perforation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right—nothing on the X-ray suggests a perforation, and your exam is not showing signs of an emergency surgical abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bariatric surgery saw me in the ER. Are they doing anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They evaluated you and recommended admission to medicine for symptom control. At this point they don’t think surgery is needed tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m in a lot of pain. The morphine helped. Can I just get that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Our goal is to control your pain, but we also want to avoid making your stomach and bowels worse. Narcotics can slow the gut and sometimes worsen abdominal symptoms. Let’s start with a non-narcotic plan: scheduled acetaminophen, your ulcer-protecting meds, and nausea medicine as needed. We’ll reassess frequently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t take NSAIDs anyway. Tylenol alone doesn’t always touch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely—no NSAIDs or aspirin given your allergy and your ulcer history. We’ll use acetaminophen on a schedule rather than only as needed, and we’ll continue your home gabapentin. We’ll also keep you on pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate to protect the stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m also worried because I feel full right after I start eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for saying that. Given your surgical history, early fullness can happen for a few reasons, but your labs and exam don’t suggest an acute blockage or infection right now. We’ll focus on symptom control and make sure you can tolerate oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been in and out of the hospital for this. Is this just going to keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot. With multiple abdominal surgeries, some people develop heightened nerve sensitivity—sometimes called visceral hyperalgesia—where pain signals are amplified even without a dangerous new problem. If that’s what’s happening, chronic pain specialists can help with longer-term strategies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you think it’s nerve pain in my belly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s one strong possibility, especially since your workup is reassuring and you’ve had similar episodes. We’ll still keep watching for anything that suggests a different cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on pyridostigmine for those eye symptoms. Could that be making my stomach worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. I also see you had outpatient neurology testing, including an EMG, that was negative for myasthenia gravis. Neurology had suggested tapering off pyridostigmine. Given your nausea and now some loose stools, we should stop it here and continue that taper plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will stopping it make my double vision worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your symptoms. Since the EMG was negative and you were already in the process of coming off it, stopping it is reasonable—especially if it’s contributing to GI upset. If your diplopia worsens significantly, we’ll reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? How’s the pain and nausea now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there. Maybe a little better after I ate some crackers. Nausea comes and goes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your vital signs are stable this morning. We’ll keep pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate on schedule, and acetaminophen regularly. We’ll also keep a bowel regimen so you don’t get backed up, since constipation can worsen pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m not constipated right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’ll tailor it—keep the baseline meds you’re already on, and we can hold or adjust if stools become too loose. The goal is steady, comfortable bowel movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had more diarrhea today. I’m worried it’s C. diff again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, that’s a reasonable concern. We’ll send a stool test for C. difficile. In the meantime, we’ll focus on hydration and watch for fever or worsening abdominal tenderness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take something to stop the diarrhea now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We usually wait until we have more information, but if you’re not having fevers and you’re otherwise stable, we can consider symptomatic treatment once we’re confident there’s no active infection. Let’s see how you do over the next several hours while the test is pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: any vomiting, blood in stool, or new severe pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Just cramps and diarrhea. Pain is still mostly on the left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit better. Still tender, but I’m eating small amounts. Diarrhea is still happening though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Your blood tests remain reassuring—no signs pointing to a new infection or a surgical emergency. Bariatric surgery also agrees there’s no role for surgery right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan if it’s not surgical?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the stomach-protecting medications, avoid medicines that can slow or upset the gut, and use a non-narcotic pain plan. For the diarrhea, once the C. diff test results are back, we can treat symptomatically if it’s negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure feels low when I stand. I’m dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. We’ll check your blood pressure lying and standing and make sure you’re hydrated. Diarrhea and poor intake can drop your pressure. Let us know before you get up so we can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. difficile PCR came back negative, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not C. diff this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—this test did not detect toxigenic C. difficile. Given that and no other signs of infection, we can treat the diarrhea symptomatically. We’ll start loperamide as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make me constipated and make the pain worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can if overused. We’ll use it only as needed—if you’re having frequent watery stools. If stools firm up, you stop it. We’ll keep your bowel regimen flexible so we’re not pushing in both directions at once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How did you do overnight with the loperamide and the pain regimen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Diarrhea slowed down. Pain is still there but not as sharp. I didn’t need morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Your labs this morning are stable, and your exam doesn’t show guarding or rebound. I think we can plan for discharge later today if you keep tolerating food and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home without stronger pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The reason we’re avoiding narcotics is that they can worsen abdominal pain over time and slow the gut. The plan is scheduled acetaminophen, continue your home gabapentin, and keep the ulcer medications consistent. We’ll also refer you to a chronic pain service to work on longer-term options for postoperative visceral pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What exactly will the pain clinic do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They can evaluate whether this fits visceral hyperalgesia and help with non-opioid strategies—medication adjustments, nerve-targeting approaches, and coping strategies—so you’re not stuck in a cycle of ER visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pyridostigmine—so I’m stopping it completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Since your outpatient EMG was negative and you were already tapering, we’re discontinuing it now, and that may also help your GI symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back for severe worsening abdominal pain, inability to keep fluids down, vomiting, blood in stool, black stools, fevers or chills, or feeling faint—especially if your blood pressure is low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, let’s review your discharge medications: continue pantoprazole twice daily, ranitidine twice daily, and sucralfate four times daily; continue your bowel regimen meds as directed; use ondansetron as needed for nausea; and use loperamide as needed for diarrhea. No narcotics at discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I keep my seizure medicine and my psych meds the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue levetiracetam for seizures, and continue your fluoxetine, aripiprazole, lorazepam, and propranolol as you were taking them. Also keep your multivitamin and iron, and atorvastatin at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Who sets up the pain clinic appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing the referral, and you’ll call to schedule with the chronic pain service physician listed in your paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’m still sore, but I feel safe to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll get your paperwork finalized. Please keep taking the ulcer medications consistently—stopping them has been associated with flares for you in the past. We’ll discharge you home now.
